## 1. Goal

Run experiments E1–E3 and turn the raw runs into the summary CSV files Ahaana's figures read: means with Student-t 95% intervals over 30 seeds, plus the raw per-job waits for the E2 CDF. The files must follow the PRD §5 summary contract exactly.

## 2. Background

**From PRD §5 Summary CSV formats:**

`tools/summarize.py` (Krishna) writes these files into `results/summaries/`. `tools/plot_figures.py` (Ahaana) reads only these files. `data/sample_summaries/` holds small, clearly fake files with exactly the same names and columns, so plotting can be built before any experiment exists. Changing any file name or column follows the §13 rule: update this section first, then code, then tell Ahaana.

**Rules for every summary file.**

- UTF-8, comma-separated, one header row, no index column, `.` as the decimal point, no thousands separators. A missing value is an empty field.
- Long format: one row per (experiment, setting, policy), plus one extra key where stated (E3 adds the priority level through `x_value`).
- Key columns, always first and in this order: `experiment` (`E1` … `E6`), `setting` (text label of the varied parameter), `x_value` (the number to put on the x-axis), `policy` (`fcfs`, `priority`, `sjf`, `aging`, `reserve`, `knapsack`), `n_seeds` (number of seeds or instances averaged; the same for every metric in the row).
- For every metric `<m>` three columns follow: `<m>_mean`, `<m>_ci_low`, `<m>_ci_high`.
- **Confidence interval.** Two-sided 95% Student-t interval of the mean across seeds: mean ± t · s / √n, with s the sample standard deviation (n − 1 in the denominator). The t value is a hard-coded constant: t(0.975, df = 29) = 2.045 for n = 30 seeds; t(0.975, df = 49) = 2.010 for the E6 groups of 50 instances. Source and rounding are recorded in `DECISIONS.md`. Any other n is an error in `summarize.py`.
- Time metrics are in ticks; utilisations are fractions from 0 to 1; ratios have no unit.

| File | Rows (key) | `setting` / `x_value` | `policy` values | Metric columns (each with `_mean`, `_ci_low`, `_ci_high`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e1_summary.csv` | (E1, load, policy) | `light` / `medium` / `heavy`; `x_value` = mean arrival rate, jobs per tick | all implemented policies | `avg_wait`, `avg_turnaround`, `util_cpu`, `util_mem` |
| `e2_summary.csv` | (E2, load, policy) | as E1 (same runs) | as E1 | `max_wait` |
| `e3_summary.csv` | (E3, priority mix, policy, priority level) | `setting` = priority mix (`uniform`, `low_heavy`, `high_heavy`); `x_value` = priority level 0–9; `n_seeds` = seeds in which that level had at least one job | `priority`, `aging` | `avg_wait` |
| `e4_summary.csv` | (E4, α, policy) | `setting` = `alpha_milli=<v>`; `x_value` = α (alpha_milli / 1000) | `aging` | `high_prio_avg_wait`, `low_prio_max_wait` (groups defined in `DECISIONS.md`) |
| `e5_summary.csv` | (E5, big-memory share, policy) | `setting` = `big_mem_pct=<v>`; `x_value` = share of big-memory jobs in percent, 0–40 | `aging`, `reserve` | `max_wait`, `avg_wait` |
| `e6_summary.csv` | (E6, job count, policy) | `setting` = `n_jobs=<v>`; `x_value` = jobs per instance, 6–9; `n_seeds` = instances (50 per job count) | all implemented policies | `turnaround_ratio`, `wait_gap` |

Two raw files feed figures that need individual values instead of means:

```csv
# e2_wait_cdf.csv: one row per job per run, for the E2 wait CDF
experiment,setting,x_value,policy,seed,job_id,wait
E2,heavy,0.9,aging,1,17,42
```

```csv
# e6_ratios.csv: one row per (instance, policy), for the E6 box plot
experiment,n_jobs,instance_seed,policy,total_turnaround,opt_total_turnaround,turnaround_ratio,total_wait,opt_total_wait,wait_gap
E6,7,1004,fcfs,212,190,1.115789,58,36,22
```

(The `#` lines above label the examples; real files have no comment lines.)

**E6 definitions.** `turnaround_ratio` = (scheduler's total turnaround) / (exact optimum's total turnaround). Total turnaround = total wait + sum of durations, so the optimal schedule is the same as for total wait, and the ratio is always defined (durations are at least 1). `wait_gap` = scheduler's total wait − optimum's total wait, in ticks (never negative). No instance is skipped. Ratios are written with six decimals.

**From BLUEPRINT §6 E1–E3:**

| # | Question | What we vary | Graph |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| E1 | Which scheduler gives the lowest average wait? | Load: light, medium, heavy (arrival rate) | Average wait vs load, one line per scheduler |
| E2 | Which scheduler prevents starvation? | Same runs as E1 | Maximum wait vs load; plus a wait distribution (CDF), as in Fan & Liang Fig. 5 |
| E3 | Are priorities respected? | Priority mix | Average wait per priority level, with and without aging. Inspired by Becker & Schüle, who report per-application flow time with and without aging in tables; we plot wait per priority level |

**From PRD §10 Python checks:**

| Check | Method | Pass condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metrics | Recompute metrics in pandas from `results.csv` | Match the C metrics JSON within 1e-9 |
| Summary format | Every file `summarize.py` writes, and every file in `data/sample_summaries/` | Exactly the §5 summary columns, in order; `ci_low ≤ mean ≤ ci_high` |

**From DECISIONS D36–D39:**

| # | Decision | Reason | Rejected alternatives | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D36 | Analysis is split: Krishna's `tools/summarize.py` writes summary CSVs to `results/summaries/`; Ahaana's `tools/plot_figures.py` reads only those files and writes `docs/report/figures/` | Clear boundary; Ahaana's code stays simple; plotting never computes statistics | One `analyze.py` doing both (previous PRD §2) | R1 |
| D37 | Summary CSVs are long format, one row per (experiment, setting, policy) (E3 adds the priority level as `x_value`), with `<metric>_mean`, `_ci_low`, `_ci_high` and one `n_seeds` column per row; plus raw `e2_wait_cdf.csv` and `e6_ratios.csv`. Exact columns in PRD §5 | Easy to filter with pandas; one contract for the plotting script | Wide format with one column per policy; a separate `n_seeds` per metric (redundant: all metrics in a row share the same seeds) | R1 |
| D38 | 95% confidence interval = two-sided Student-t interval of the mean: mean ± t·s/√n. Hard-coded constants: t(0.975, 29) = 2.045 (n = 30 seeds) and t(0.975, 49) = 2.010 (E6 groups of 50 instances), both rounded to 3 decimals. Source: standard table of critical values of the t distribution, NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods §1.3.6.7.2 (**verify the two table values before Gate 3**) | No SciPy dependency; Ahaana's code never computes statistics | Bootstrap intervals; normal approximation (1.96); SciPy | R1 |
| D39 | Any n other than 30 or 50 in `summarize.py` is an error, not a guess | Keeps the hard-coded constants honest | Interpolating t values | R1 |

## 3. Scope

**In scope:**

- E1/E2 grid (light, medium, heavy) and E3 grid (priority mixes) in `tools/config.py`, 30 seeds each
- `summarize.py` computing mean, ci_low, ci_high per metric with the hard-coded t values
- Writing the four files into `results/summaries/`
- Verifying the t constants against the cited table before use (D38) and noting it in the PR
- `tests/py/test_summaries.py` (format checks on real and sample files, metric recomputation)

**Out of scope:**

- Figures (A-03)
- E4–E6 (K-28, K-35)
- Any statistic not in PRD §5

## 5. Specification

Interval: mean ± t·s/√n with s the sample standard deviation (n − 1); t = 2.045 for n = 30 (df 29); t = 2.010 for n = 50 (df 49); any other n raises an error (D39).

Per-seed values first, then summarise across seeds: for each (setting, policy, seed) compute the run's avg_wait, avg_turnaround, util_cpu, util_mem, max_wait from `results.csv`/`metrics.json`; then mean and interval over the 30 seeds. E3: per (mix, policy, priority level), mean over seeds in which that level had at least one job; `n_seeds` counts those seeds (t value for that n must exist, otherwise raise and report — never guess).

`e2_wait_cdf.csv`: every job's wait from every E2 run (`experiment,setting,x_value,policy,seed,job_id,wait`).

## 9. How to verify

```sh
python tools/run_experiments.py --experiment E1 && python tools/run_experiments.py --experiment E3
python tools/summarize.py --experiments E1 E2 E3
pytest tests/py/test_summaries.py -q
```

## 10. Viva notes

**Idea:** each seed gives one measurement; the interval says how far the true mean could plausibly be from our average of 30.
**Why Student-t, not 1.96?** With 30 samples the standard deviation is itself estimated, so the t distribution (wider) is correct.
**Examiner question:** "What does the error bar mean?" — If we repeated the 30-seed experiment many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean.

## 11. Pitfalls

- Averaging all jobs from all seeds together (wrong unit: the seed is the sample)
- Population std (ddof=0) instead of sample std
- Committing `results/`
